The average radar cross-section of large birds is around -20 dBm2 at 10 GHz.
A sample calculation shows a generic pulsed radar system could detect birds up to a range of 3.8 km.
A sample FMCW radar system could detect birds up to a range of 4.8 km.
The SCOUT radar used in the experiments was modified from FM-CW mode to CW mode.
The SCOUT radar data was sampled at a rate of 100 kHz.
The Flycatcher search-and-tracking radar system was used to aim and track the targets for the SCOUT and IRSCAN systems.
The IRSCAN infrared surveillance system was used to provide video of the targets in the radar beam.
Interfering signals from other radar systems significantly disturbed the SCOUT radar data.
Groups of birds caused multiple Doppler frequencies in the spectra due to their individual velocities and flight directions.
Seagulls exhibited a characteristic hovering flight pattern in the radar data.
Some birds showed small frequency components on both sides of the main body line in the spectrum, but the origin was unclear.
The paper notes that further research is needed to develop reliable methods for classifying birds using radar data.
The measurements were conducted on October 29, 1992 as part of the ARTIST trials.
The SCOUT radar operated in the X-band at a frequency of 9 GHz.
The Doppler frequency shift was calculated using the formula f_Doppler = 60v_r, where v_r is the radial velocity.
